titre: The First Proof No One Could Reread
accroche: In 1976, a computer settles a 124-year-old problem. The community splits over what a proof is
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1852, a London student named Francis Guthrie colors a map of the counties of England. He wants two neighboring counties never to receive the same color, and finds that four always suffice. He asks his brother whether this is chance. The question reaches the mathematician Augustus De Morgan, then circulates.

It looks like an exercise. It will resist for one hundred twenty-four years.

## What Makes the Statement Tough

Checking that a given map can be colored with four colors is easy. Proving that no map, among infinitely many possible maps, requires five is of another order.

Two false proofs were published and accepted; the one by Alfred Kempe, in 1879, held for eleven years before a flaw was found in it. Kempe's idea nonetheless survives his proof, and it structures everything that follows. The aim is to find an *unavoidable* set of configurations, that is, a catalog of patterns such that every map contains at least one of them; and then to show that each of these patterns is *reducible*: if it appears, we know how to reduce the problem to a smaller map.

If the catalog is finite, the proof closes by induction. The whole difficulty is building it.

## A Month of Computation

In 1976, at the University of Illinois, Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken succeed, with John Koch for the computing part. Their catalog has 1,482 configurations in its published version, and checking their reducibility takes more than a month of machine time.

The proof appears in two parts in the Illinois Journal of Mathematics the following year. It is correct. It is also unreadable: no mathematician can follow the enumeration of cases by hand.

## What Became of the Idea of Proof

The community splits, and the disagreement is not about the result. It is about what we expect of a proof.

A proof has never had the sole function of establishing that a statement is true. It also serves to make us understand *why* it is, and an enumeration of 1,482 cases explains nothing. The objection has remained intact: the theorem is established, understanding is still lacking.

The other objection, the one about reliability, received its answer in 2005. Georges Gonthier and Benjamin Werner rebuilt the entire proof in the Coq proof assistant, combinatorial part included, so that its correctness now rests only on a verification kernel of a few thousand lines.

Doubt has thus changed its object rather than disappeared. We no longer trust a program that enumerates cases; we trust a program that checks proofs. Computer-assisted proofs have since become ordinary, and the question posed in 1976, is a proof that no human can walk through still a proof?, has never received a clear-cut answer.

repere.texte: Appel and Haken's proof appears in two parts in the Illinois Journal of Mathematics in 1977; the computer verification had taken more than a month of machine time.
repere.source: Appel & Haken, “Every Planar Map is Four Colorable,” Illinois Journal of Mathematics, 21, 1977

carte.punch: A proof no mathematician can follow by hand: 1,482 cases checked by computer.
carte.idee: Four colors suffice to color any map without two neighbors looking alike. Appel and Haken proved it in 1976: a computer checked 1,482 configurations over more than a month of machine time. The proof is correct, but unreadable by hand.

quiz.question: Why was the 1976 proof contested?
choix: Because it left out maps with enclaves
Because a calculation error was discovered in it a few years later
Because no human could check the enumeration of cases by hand
Because it only held for flat maps, and not on the surface of a sphere
quiz.explication: The contestation was not about the result, which has never been faulted, but about the status of a proof whose decisive part is beyond the reach of human reading, hence the double objection: reliability, and the absence of explanation. The 2005 formalization in Coq answered the first, not the second. The case of the sphere, for its part, is equivalent to that of the plane.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does it all begin, in 1852, with Francis Guthrie?
choix: He is looking for a mathematical proof for a university competition
He colors a map of the counties of England and notices that four colors always suffice
He tries to prove a theorem already known in Euclidean geometry
He is working on a military mapmaking problem commissioned by the British army
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Guthrie colors a map of the counties of England, wanting two neighboring counties never to have the same color, and finds that four colors always suffice.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is an "unavoidable" set of configurations, in the proof strategy inherited from Kempe?
choix: A catalog of patterns such that every map necessarily contains at least one of them
A list of maps that no proof can ever solve
A set of colors that it is impossible to avoid using
A sequence of calculations that the computer cannot fully verify
quiz_supplementaire.explication: An unavoidable set is a catalog of patterns such that every map contains at least one of them; one must then show that each of these patterns is reducible.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the reconstruction of the proof by Gonthier and Werner in the Coq proof assistant, in 2005, make it possible to establish?
choix: Reducing the theorem to only three necessary colors instead of four
Entirely replacing computing with purely manual reasoning
Making the proof's reliability rest on a verification kernel of a few thousand lines
Demonstrating that Appel and Haken's proof actually contained an error
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The reconstruction in Coq makes the correctness of the proof rest on a verification kernel of a few thousand lines, answering the objection about reliability.
